stories.title: Israeli strike kills 2 senior Hamas officials
stories.dek: The second strike left four people dead, including two children.
stories.content:
Mourners carry the bodies of Muhammad Abu al-Ouf, a Hamas internal security officer, and his family, during their funeral in Gaza City. They were killed in an Israeli strike. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press) Social Sharing It was a chaotic scene in the Al Shati refugee camp in Gaza City after an Israeli strike hit an apartment building, leaving four dead and multiple injuries. It shattered the facade and left furniture and toys strewn on the ground.

Witnesses say multiple people were sheltering nearby and the strike came with no prior notice.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said they were targeting a senior Hamas security official who was sheltering in the building with his wife and two children. Mohammad Abuelouf was a Hamas colonel who headed the militant’s internal security service in northern Gaza.

It was the second senior Hamas security official killed in the last 24 hours. Yesterday afternoon, IDF targeted Naim Abu Nahal in a displacement camp in Gaza City — he was also the head of security.

A Palestinian man inspects an apartment destroyed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

IDF strikes have continued throughout the ceasefire as Israel insists it will go after Hamas officials until they lay down their arms. Peace talks have not moved beyond the first phase announced last October and both sides blame the other for the lack of progress.

Mahmoud Bakr, 33, was sheltering near the site of the strike when the explosion happened. He says there’s no safety in Gaza.

"This is what you call a ceasefire?" he told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife. "If, while we’re sleeping bombs fall on us, then where is the ceasefire?"

The Israeli military confirmed it had killed Abuelouf, whom it described as a ​significant figure who "served as a key source of expertise in efforts to restrict the IDF’s ⁠counterterrorism operations in the Gaza Strip."

Despite a year-old ceasefire, Israel has continued to carry out attacks that it ​says target Hamas but have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by U.S. President Donald Trump, ​has not halted the violence or secured Hamas's disarmament.

Palestinian children look at an apartment destroyed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Medics said Wednesday's airstrike had ripped through Abuelouf's apartment in the Beach refugee camp in western Gaza City, near the coast. Later in the morning, another Israeli airstrike hit Gaza City's northern Karama neighbourhood, killing one person, medics said.

stories.title: Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize
stories.dek: Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an …
stories.content:
Freelance journalist Mariam Dagga, 33, was renownn for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the Gaza war. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP View image in fullscreen Freelance journalist Mariam Dagga, 33, was renownn for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the Gaza war. Photograph: Jehad Alshrafi/AP War reporting Palestinian journalist killed by Israel in Gaza wins Rory Peck prize Mariam Dagga shares award with two of her colleagues from AP for ‘powerful coverage’ of human cost of war

Mariam Dagga, the Palestinian war correspondent who was killed at the age of 33 in Gaza in an Israeli strike, has posthumously won the prestigious Rory Peck prize for freelance video journalists, the organisers announced on Wednesday.

She shares the award with two of her colleagues from the Associated Press (AP), Abdel Kareem Hana and Jehad Alshrafi, “for their powerful coverage of the human cost of the war” in the Palestinian territory, the Rory Peck Trust said.

Dagga, who has a teenage son named Ghaith, was killed in August 2025 in an Israeli airstrike on a southern Gaza hospital , which claimed the lives of four other journalists.

The independent photographer and reporter had been working with the AP news agency since the beginning of the current conflict, triggered by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.

Dagga was renowned for her relentless reporting despite the personal losses she suffered throughout the war. She filmed the death of a protester who was shot during the 2018 Great March of Return in Gaza , when Israeli forces shot protesters marching towards the Gaza border fence, killing more than 220 people and wounding more than 9,200. She later discovered that the protester was her brother.

The war correspondent continued her work as a journalist during the war in Gaza over the last 22 months, working as a freelancer with the AP and Independent Arabia.

View image in fullscreen Mariam Dagga’s father holds a camera and mobile phone belonging to his daughter after she was killed in August 2025. Photograph: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP The AP’s executive editor, Julie Pace, said: “Journalists play an essential role in documenting events and informing the public, often at enormous personal risk.

“We honour Mariam and all journalists killed during this conflict and other conflicts – and remain committed to seeking answers about their deaths.”

stories.title: Uttariya instead of robes: West Bengal Government suggests universities to adopt Indian attire in convocations
stories.dek: West Bengal Higher Education Minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay said that the government was putting effort to follow own Indian culture and tradition and Uttariyo is enough for such ceremonies
stories.content:
Account subscription benefits alongside Premium Stories, Editorials, Opinions and more. Unlock these with Subscription

The View From India Looking at World Affairs from the Indian perspective.

First Day First Show News and reviews from the world of cinema and streaming.

Today's Cache Your download of the top 5 technology stories of the day.

Health Matters Ramya Kannan writes to you on getting to good health, and staying there

West Bengal Higher Education Department has advised all the State-aided universities to adopt Indian attire such as Uttariya and clothes made of handloom fabric instead of Western robes during convocation or any academic ceremony.

“We are putting effort to follow our own Indian culture and tradition. Uttariyo is enough for such ceremonies. Why do we have to wear robes? Many institutions, including the Indian Institute of Technology [IIT], have adopted only uttariya. Hence, we made the suggestion,” West Bengal Higher Education Minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay told media persons on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).

The development also came days after Mr. Chattopadhyay praised the Jalpaiguri Government Engineering College for upholding Indian traditions by replacing the conventional academic gown with a traditional uttariya.

“As we strive to build a self-reliant Bharat, our education system must also reflect our civilisational values and cultural identity,” he wrote on X congratulating the students of the college.

In its notice sent to all the vice chancellors of the universities, the department has now said that the UGC had not prescribed any rigid uniform design for ceremonial robes.

Hence, the universities have the flexibility to incorporate traditional Indian attire, such as the uttariya, and to design distinct ceremonial attire for dignitaries and degree recipients.

Monday’s (November 23) notice to the VCs said that the ceremonial attire made from Indian handloom was more suited to India’s climate. Such a preference for handloom fabrics and traditional Indian attire also supports the rural handloom industry and weavers’ livelihoods, it said.

“In view of the above, you are requested to take necessary steps to consider adopting handloom fabrics and traditional attire for the academic robes worn during convocation in your esteemed university as well as affiliated colleges, wherever applicable,” the department stated in the advisory asking the universities to send to confirmation of the communication to the department.

stories.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
stories.dek: The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
stories.content:
The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.

Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.

That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.

The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)

stories.title: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism
stories.dek: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave.
stories.content:
A surprisingly simple metal has revealed an unusual form of magnetism that could open new possibilities for quantum technology. Researchers have found compelling evidence of a rare magnetic state in which electrons behave in unexpected ways, even though the material produces no overall magnetization.

The material, known as europium silicide (EuSi), contains an intricate magnetic structure that influences how electrons move and how their spins are oriented. This behavior is associated with a phenomenon called p-wave magnetism, an emerging area of research that could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to controlling electronic properties.

The discovery is particularly significant because EuSi is a relatively simple metallic compound. Unlike many materials previously considered for studying this exotic form of magnetism, it offers researchers a practical way to investigate the underlying physics in detail.

The research began about three years ago at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Physics of Solids (MPI CPfS) in Dresden, Germany. Dr. Erjian Cheng successfully grew high-quality single crystals of EuSi, providing the material needed for detailed experiments.

When researchers first examined the crystals using photoemission techniques, which probe the energies and behavior of electrons inside materials, they noticed something unexpected. The magnetic arrangement of the atoms had a remarkably strong influence on the electronic band structure, which describes the energy levels electrons can occupy and helps determine how a material conducts electricity.

That observation raised an intriguing possibility. Could this simple compound contain an unconventional form of magnetism in which the spin of an electron is connected to the direction it travels?

"When we first measured the electronic structure of EuSi, we were surprised by the exceptionally large effect of magnetism on the electrons," explains Cheng. "That observation led us to investigate whether this simple compound could host a much more unusual magnetic state. The combination of crystal growth, neutron scattering and spin-resolved spectroscopy now provides compelling evidence for p-wave magnetism."

Answering that question required an international collaboration involving 38 scientists from 19 institutions. Participants included researchers from ShanghaiTech University, the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

Ordinary magnets, such as those attached to refrigerators, typically rely on a magnetic arrangement called ferromagnetism. In these materials, many electron spins align in the same direction, producing an overall magnetic field.

stories.title: Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Agreements and Regional Energy Corridors
stories.dek: A multi-perspective assessment of offshore natural gas transit frameworks, maritime boundary negotiations, and regional stability.
stories.content:
The Eastern Mediterranean basin continues to navigate complex multilateral diplomatic engagements balancing offshore energy exploration with sovereign boundary delimitation. High-level delegations from regional coastal states and European partners are refining frameworks that align pipeline routes with equitable maritime economic zones.

Key Perspectives & Strategic Dimensions:
1. Energy Transit Security: Multilateral agreements between Mediterranean states prioritize uninterrupted transit of natural gas to Southern European ports, diversifying continental supply lines.
2. Maritime Boundary Delimitation: Diplomatic mediators emphasize that long-term maritime stability necessitates transparent dispute-resolution mechanisms that account for sovereign continental shelf claims.
3. Regional Economic Interdependence: Joint infrastructure investments in subsea interconnectors create economic mutual interest, offering pragmatic stabilization incentives across diverse stakeholders.
stories.whyItMatters: Directly impacts the economic stability, energy infrastructure, and security landscape across the Levant and Mediterranean.

stories.title: Sub-Microsecond Spin Dynamics in Diamond NV Centers: Benchmarking Cavity QED and Coherence Limits
stories.dek: Mitigating dipolar spin-spin dephasing and hyperfine bath interactions in dense diamond NV ensembles via Floquet driving.
stories.content:
Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color centers in diamond remain the preeminent solid-state platform for room-temperature quantum metrology and nanoscale magnetic resonance. Scaling from isolated defects to dense ensembles requires overcoming collective dephasing from the surrounding 13C nuclear spin bath.

Recent breakthroughs utilizing microwave cavity coupling and Floquet dynamical decoupling extend the effective coherence time (T2*) by an order of magnitude.

Key Technical Highlights:
1. Cooperative Purcell Enhancement: Dense NV ensembles entering the collective strong coupling regime demonstrate cavity-mediated coherence preservation.
2. Suppression of Spin-Diffusion Loss: Operating within crystallographic symmetry subspaces eliminates cross-axis relaxation.
3. Room-Temperature Sensing: Sustained microsecond coherence enables sub-picotesla magnetic field sensitivities for single-cell NMR.
stories.whyItMatters: Informs room-temperature diamond quantum magnetometry, microwave cavity loading, and advanced Floquet decoupling protocols in spin dynamics.

stories.source: Innatera & Edge AI Insights • 5 min read
stories.title: Sub-Milliwatt Neuromorphic Microcontrollers Shift Real-Time AI Inference to the Edge
stories.dek: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) on silicon processors achieve microsecond response times at sub-milliwatt power budgets.
stories.content:
The paradigm of routing sensor telemetry to centralized cloud servers is rapidly transitioning to on-device neuromorphic microcontrollers. Utilizing event-driven spiking neural architectures, silicon accelerators process acoustic and vibration patterns with near-zero latency.

Key Highlights:
1. In-Memory Processing: Spiking architectures circumvent the classical von Neumann memory bottleneck, consuming less than 1 mW.
2. Zero Cloud Exposure: Sensitive sensor streams remain strictly local, guaranteeing privacy and continuous operation during network blackouts.
3. Predictive Maintenance: Deployed microcontrollers classify industrial vibrations and structural stress in real time.
stories.whyItMatters: Enables zero-latency, private, on-device anomaly detection and vibration monitoring without cloud roundtrips.

stories.title: Circadian Photonic Priming and Equanimity in Demanding Research
stories.dek: Aligning 90-minute ultradian deep work blocks with natural circadian rhythms and secular Buddhist non-reactivity.
stories.content:
Sustained high-level analytical performance requires deliberate biological pacing. Structuring the day around 90-minute ultradian cycles followed by brief decompression intervals prevents cognitive fatigue.

Core Evidence-Based Habits:
1. Photonic Lock: Direct outdoor light exposure within 45 minutes of waking aligns the suprachiasmatic nucleus master clock.
2. Ultradian Block: Dedicate the primary 9:00 AM - 10:30 AM window to pure theoretical derivation before checking correspondence.
3. Secular Equanimity (Dhammapada 81): 'Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.'
stories.whyItMatters: Protects cognitive bandwidth and prevents attentional fragmentation during demanding laboratory derivations.

papers.title: Systematically improvable semiclassical clustering for accurate and efficient quantum dynamics in large spin ensembles
papers.tldr: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies. While accurate methods for spin dynamics are limited to relatively small systems, the dissipative spin environments in real experiments typically involve orders of magnitude more spins.
takeaways: Predicting the decoherence of spin qubits in realistic environments is key to identifying the interactions that limit their coherence---a prerequisite for designing better quantum technologies.
We show that our method is applicable to systems containing arbitrary spin species under dynamical decoupling pulse sequences.

We demonstrate that cluster spin-LSC recovers numerically exact coherence and population dynamics for a nitrogen-vacancy center and a molecular qubit, reducing day-long multi-GPU simulations to only minutes on a CPU.

papers.title: Signatures of Kitaev quantum spin liquid states in $α$-RuCl$_3$ revealed by nitrogen-vacancy spin-noise spectroscopy
papers.authors: Jitender Kumar, Sehrish Iqbal, Himani Saraswat et al.
papers.tldr: Bond-dependent magnetic interactions, strong spin-orbit coupling, and quantum fluctuations in $α$-RuCl$_3$ make it an archetypical candidate for exotic Kitaev quantum spin liquid (QSL) states. While electronic transport, neutron scattering, optical and tunneling spectroscopies were used to probe global QSL signatures in large scale $α$-RuCl$_3$ samples, nanoscale evidence of local QSL behavior via a non-invasive experimental probe is still missing.
takeaways: Here, we use diamond nitrogen-vacancy (NV) spin-noise spectroscopy to probe QSL states in α-RuCl3 nanoflakes with thicknesses ranging from 8 to 150 nm over a temperature range of 4.3-250 K.

Our measurements reveal a pronounced decrease in the NV spin-lattice relaxation time ($T_{1}$) below ~100 K in proximity to the $α$-RuCl$_3$ flakes, indicating enhanced GHz-frequency magnetic fluctuations.

These results establish NV spin-noise spectroscopy as a local, non-invasive probe of low-energy spin dynamics in $α$-RuCl$_3$ nanoflakes and open a route to testing predicted noise signatures of fractionalized excitations in atomically thin QSL candidates.

papers.title: Bright and Uniform Silicon Carbide Nanophotonic Arrays for Scalable Nanoscale Quantum Sensing
papers.authors: Chenyang Liao, Chihang Luo, Xin Chen et al.
papers.tldr: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility. However, poor photon collection efficiency and the reliance on randomly distributed defects hinder the realization of practical, large-scale devices.
takeaways: Silicon carbide (SiC) spin defects are emerging as powerful platforms for nanoscale quantum sensing due to their near-surface stability, near-infrared emission, and CMOS compatibility.
Furthermore, we apply these devices to nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), successfully demonstrating external nanoscale nuclear-spin detection.
These results establish our SiC nanopillars as robust building blocks for scanning quantum probes and scalable sensor networks.

papers.title: Quantum Control Under Control-Dependent Decoherence
papers.authors: Cyril Morluyan Cordor, Anthony M. Bloch, Eitan Geva
papers.tldr: Decoherence, which arises from the interaction of a quantum system with a typically much larger thermal environment, or bath, poses major challenges to the controllability of quantum systems. The dynamics of such open quantum systems is often represented by Markovian quantum master equations of the Lindblad or Redfield type.
takeaways: Decoherence, which arises from the interaction of a quantum system with a typically much larger thermal environment, or bath, poses major challenges to the controllability of quantum systems.
The dynamics of such open quantum systems is often represented by Markovian quantum master equations of the Lindblad or Redfield type.
To this end, we examine the effect of accounting for control-dependent decoherence on the controllability of an open quantum system in the case of a two-level system coupled to a thermal bath.

papers.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
papers.tldr: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts.
takeaways: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout.
We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble.
We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.
